## Build Your Own Palette · Step 2: the ECON ramps {.smaller}

[Theme builder · palette]{.eyebrow}

### Nine named ramps cover qualitative + sequential needs

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
For many-category and continuous data, the five aren't enough. Drop in **nine
named ramps** — each a dark-to-light gradient — so any chart can pick a ramp by
city name.

```python {code-line-numbers="1-7"}
ECON = {
    "chicago":   ["#141F52", ..., "#EBEDFA"],
    "hongkong":  ["#169C7F", ..., "#E9FCF8"],
    "newyork":   ["#F9C31F", ..., "#FEF8E6"],
    "shanghai":  ["#4C9C16", ..., "#F0FCE9"],
    "tokyo":     ["#9C1633", ..., "#FCE9ED"],
    # singapore, red, london (grey), canvas
}
```
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.5
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4.5))
max_len = max(len(r) for r in ECON.values())
for j, (name, ramp) in enumerate(ECON.items()):
    for i, hex in enumerate(ramp):
        ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((i, -j), 0.95, 0.9, color=hex, ec=CREAM, lw=0.6))
    ax.text(-0.2, -j + 0.45, name, ha="right", va="center",
            fontsize=9, color=INK, family="IBM Plex Mono")
ax.set_xlim(-2.5, max_len); ax.set_ylim(-len(ECON) + 0.5, 1)
ax.axis("off")
ax.set_title("ECON RAMPS", fontsize=11, fontweight="bold", color=INK, pad=6)
plt.show()
```
:::
::::


<!-- slide 49 -->
## Build Your Own Palette · Step 3: continuous cmaps {.smaller}

[Theme builder · palette]{.eyebrow}

### Three helpers turn the ramps into matplotlib colormaps

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
For heatmaps and stacked areas you want a *continuous* gradient.
`LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list` interpolates between any list of hexes.

```python {code-line-numbers="1-12"}
from matplotlib.colors \
    import LinearSegmentedColormap

def econ_cmap(ramp="chicago"):
    return LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list(
        f"econ_{ramp}", ECON[ramp])

econ_diverging = LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list(
    "econ_div", [BLUE, CREAM, RED])

econ_spectrum = LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list(
    "econ_spectrum",
    [ECON["chicago"][2], ECON["hongkong"][0],
     ECON["shanghai"][1], ECON["newyork"][0],
     ECON["red"][1]])
```
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.6
import numpy as np
fig, ax = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(7, 3.6))
gradient = np.linspace(0, 1, 256).reshape(1, -1)
demos = [(econ_cmap("chicago"),     "econ_cmap('chicago')   — sequential"),
         (econ_diverging,            "econ_diverging         — blue ←→ red"),
         (econ_spectrum,             "econ_spectrum          — blue → red")]
for a, (cmap, name) in zip(ax, demos):
    a.imshow(gradient, aspect="auto", cmap=cmap)
    a.set_yticks([]); a.set_xticks([])
    a.set_title(name, fontsize=10, color=INK, loc="left",
                family="IBM Plex Mono", pad=4)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
:::
::::


<!-- slide 50 -->
## Build Your Own Theme · Step 1: register IBM Plex Mono {.smaller}

[Theme builder · font]{.eyebrow}

### Tell matplotlib about the .ttf files, set it as the default

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
The repo ships `fonts/IBM_Plex_Mono/`. Walk the folder, add each `.ttf` to
matplotlib's font manager, and remember the family name. A fallback keeps the
render alive if the folder ever moves.

```python {code-line-numbers="1-12"}
from pathlib import Path
import matplotlib.font_manager as fm

font_dir = Path("../fonts/IBM_Plex_Mono")
if font_dir.exists():
    for ttf in font_dir.glob("*.ttf"):
        fm.fontManager.addfont(str(ttf))
    _MONO = "IBM Plex Mono"
else:
    _MONO = "DejaVu Sans Mono"   # safe fallback
```
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
ax.axis("off")
ax.text(0.5, 0.78, "IBM Plex Mono", ha="center", va="center",
        fontsize=32, fontweight="bold", color=GREEN,
        family="IBM Plex Mono")
ax.text(0.5, 0.55, "registered, available everywhere",
        ha="center", va="center", fontsize=14, color=INK,
        family="IBM Plex Mono")
ax.text(0.5, 0.30, "ax.set_title(\"BRCA1 expression\")",
        ha="center", va="center", fontsize=12, color=MUTED,
        family="IBM Plex Mono")
ax.text(0.5, 0.12, "↳ now in IBM Plex Mono by default",
        ha="center", va="center", fontsize=10, color=GREY,
        family="IBM Plex Mono", style="italic")
plt.show()
```
:::
::::


<!-- slide 51 -->
## Build Your Own Theme · Step 2: rcParams once {.smaller}

[Theme builder · rcParams]{.eyebrow}

### Set every default once; inherit it forever

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
A single `rcParams.update` call sets the cream canvas, muted axes, and IBM Plex
Mono as the matplotlib default. Every later figure inherits it — no per-chunk
boilerplate.

```python {code-line-numbers="1-10"}
import matplotlib as mpl

mpl.rcParams.update({
    "figure.facecolor": CREAM,
    "axes.facecolor":   CREAM,
    "savefig.facecolor": CREAM,
    "font.family":      _MONO,
    "axes.edgecolor":   LINE,
    "axes.labelcolor":  MUTED,
    "xtick.color":      MUTED,
    "ytick.color":      MUTED,
    "axes.spines.top":   False,
    "axes.spines.right": False,
})
```
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.4
genes = ["BRCA1", "TP53", "EGFR", "MYC", "KRAS"]
vals = [72, 58, 85, 63, 91]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4.4))
ax.barh(genes[::-1], vals[::-1], color=GREEN, height=0.62)
for i, v in enumerate(vals[::-1]):
    ax.text(v + 1, i, str(v), va="center", fontsize=10, color=MUTED)
ax.set_xlim(0, 105)
ax.set_xlabel("Expression (TPM)")
for s in ["top", "right", "bottom"]: ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
ax.xaxis.set_visible(False)
ax.set_title("EVERY DEFAULT SET, NOTHING REPEATED",
             fontsize=12, fontweight="bold", color=INK, pad=10)
plt.show()
```
:::
::::


<!-- slide 52 -->
## The Whole Theme in One Line {.smaller}

[Theme builder · the payoff]{.eyebrow}

### `from genomics_course.theme import *`

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
You've just seen the inside of `genomics_course/theme.py`. The deck itself never
re-declares the palette or font — it just imports the same module:

```python
from genomics_course.theme import *
```

That single line brings in **`GREEN BLUE AMBER RED PURPLE`** plus the
neutrals, the `ECON` ramps, the helpers (`econ_cmap`, `econ_diverging`,
`econ_spectrum`), and applies the cream-canvas rcParams. Every figure in
**Day 1 through Day 3** inherits the same look.

That's the recipe: **palette → font → rcParams → one import line.**
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.4
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4.4))
ax.axis("off")
ax.text(0.5, 0.82, "from genomics_course.theme import *",
        ha="center", va="center", fontsize=18, fontweight="bold",
        color=GREEN, family="IBM Plex Mono",
        bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.6", fc=ECON["hongkong"][3],
                  ec=GREEN, lw=1.4))
items = [
    ("•", "five story colours",              GREEN),
    ("•", "nine named ECON ramps",           BLUE),
    ("•", "econ_cmap / diverging / spectrum", AMBER),
    ("•", "IBM Plex Mono registered",        PURPLE),
    ("•", "cream canvas + muted axes",       RED),
]
for i, (bul, text, c) in enumerate(items):
    y = 0.55 - i * 0.09
    ax.text(0.15, y, bul, ha="center", va="center",
            fontsize=18, fontweight="bold", color=c)
    ax.text(0.20, y, text, ha="left", va="center",
            fontsize=12, color=INK, family="IBM Plex Mono")
plt.show()
```
:::
::::

::: {.takeaway}
One line, one identity. Every figure in the deck shares it; every figure in
your work can share it too.
:::



<!-- slide 53 -->
## The Three Objects Behind a Theme {.smaller}

[Make it publication-ready]{.eyebrow}

### A palette, an rcParams block, and per-plot tuning

::: {.full-width-lead}
Publication style is not magic per chart. It is three objects: design tokens you pick once, an `rcParams` block that makes them the default everywhere, and the `ax.set_*` calls you tune per figure. That is all `theme.py` is.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset}

### 1 · Palette + font

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
Pick a few colours and one typeface, name them as constants. One bold colour to carry the story, the rest quiet neutrals. These are your tokens, nothing renders yet.

```{.python code-line-numbers="2,8"}
# story colours
GREEN = "#379A8B"
BLUE  = "#006BA2"
RED   = "#B4405F"
# neutrals
INK   = "#0D0D0D"
MUTED = "#666666"
GREY  = "#B3B3B3"
```
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4.4
swatch = [("GREEN", GREEN), ("BLUE", BLUE), ("AMBER", AMBER),
          ("RED", RED), ("PURPLE", PURPLE), ("INK", INK),
          ("LINE", LINE), ("MUTED", MUTED), ("GREY", GREY), ("CREAM", CREAM)]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4.4), facecolor=CREAM); ax.set_facecolor(CREAM)
for i, (name, hexv) in enumerate(swatch):
    y = len(swatch) - 1 - i
    ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((0, y), 1.1, 0.8, color=hexv,
                 ec=LINE if name in ("CREAM", "LINE") else "none", lw=0.8))
    ax.text(1.3, y + 0.4, name, va="center", fontweight="bold", color=INK)
    ax.text(2.7, y + 0.4, hexv, va="center", color=MUTED)
ax.set_xlim(0, 4); ax.set_ylim(0, len(swatch)); ax.axis("off")
plt.show()
```
:::
::::

### 2 · rcParams

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
Push the tokens into `plt.rcParams` once. Now every plot inherits the font, the cream canvas, thinned spines, and a quiet grid, with no per-plot styling at all. This is the same figure tab 3 will label.

```{.python code-line-numbers="1|3-6"}
plt.rcParams.update({
    "font.family": "IBM Plex Mono",
    "figure.facecolor": CREAM,
    "axes.facecolor": CREAM,
    "axes.spines.top": False,
    "axes.spines.right": False,
    "axes.edgecolor": LINE,
    "axes.labelcolor": MUTED,
    "grid.color": LINE,
    "grid.alpha": 0.4,
})
```
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 6.4
#| fig-height: 4.4
x = np.linspace(0, 10, 50)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 4.4), facecolor=CREAM)
ax.set_facecolor(CREAM)
for k, c in zip((1, 1.5, 2), (GREEN, BLUE, AMBER)):
    ax.plot(x, np.sin(x*0.6)*k + k, color=c, lw=2.2)
ax.grid(True, color=LINE, alpha=0.5, linewidth=0.6); ax.set_axisbelow(True)
for s in ("top", "right"): ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
for s in ("left", "bottom"): ax.spines[s].set_color(LINE)
ax.tick_params(colors=MUTED)
plt.show()
```
:::
::::

### 3 · ax.set_* (per plot)

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
Same curves, same theme, now named for *this* figure. `ax.set_*` is the only thing you touch per plot: the title, the axis labels, the limits. The layer on top of the inherited defaults.

```{.python code-line-numbers="5-7"}
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
for k, c in zip((1, 1.5, 2), (GREEN, BLUE, AMBER)):
    ax.plot(x, np.sin(x*0.6)*k + k, color=c)

ax.set_title("Three signals over time")
ax.set_xlabel("time (s)")
ax.set_ylabel("amplitude")
```
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 6.4
#| fig-height: 4.4
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 4.4), facecolor=CREAM)
ax.set_facecolor(CREAM)
for k, c in zip((1, 1.5, 2), (GREEN, BLUE, AMBER)):
    ax.plot(x, np.sin(x*0.6)*k + k, color=c, lw=2.2)
ax.set_title("Three signals over time", fontweight="bold", color=INK, loc="left")
ax.set_xlabel("time (s)")
ax.set_ylabel("amplitude")
ax.grid(True, color=LINE, alpha=0.5, linewidth=0.6); ax.set_axisbelow(True)
for s in ("top", "right"): ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
for s in ("left", "bottom"): ax.spines[s].set_color(LINE)
ax.tick_params(colors=MUTED)
plt.show()
```
:::
::::

:::

<!-- slide 54 -->
## Theme It Once, Then Tune {.smaller}

[Make it publication-ready]{.eyebrow}

### The bottom line, and three things to try

::: {.takeaway}
[The bottom line]{.tl}
Set the **palette and rcParams once** in `theme.py`, then every plot starts publication-ready. `ax.set_*` is all you touch per figure.
:::

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Q1 · Italicise one word in a title**
How do you make only *gaining* italic in "Mixed training is gaining"?

::: {.fragment}
Mathtext, not rcParams:
```python
ax.set_title(r"Mixed training is $\it{gaining}$")
```
:::

**Q2 · One plot off-theme**
Your theme is global. How do you make a single plot use a white background without changing the others?

::: {.fragment}
Scope it with a context manager:
```python
with mpl.rc_context({"axes.facecolor": "white"}):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots()
```
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Q3 · Style only the x-axis font**
rcParams sets the font everywhere. How do you change it on the x-ticks alone?

::: {.fragment}
A per-axis call:
```python
ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelfontfamily="serif")
```
:::

**Q4 · You broke your rcParams**
You experimented in a notebook and every plot looks wrong. How do you get back to defaults?

::: {.fragment}
One line resets the lot:
```python
import matplotlib as mpl
mpl.rcdefaults()
```
:::
:::
::::::

<!-- slide 55 -->
## Make matplotlib publication-ready {.smaller .scrollable}

[Make it publication-ready]{.eyebrow}

### Five small moves take matplotlib from default to glorious

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
Default matplotlib is functional. Five small moves take it to publication-ready:
one **bold** colour carries the story, the frame thins out, the grid quiets, the
bars label themselves, and a descriptive title says what the chart shows.

```python {code-line-numbers="3-5|7-9|11-12|14-17|19-22"}
# 1) STRATEGIC COLOUR — one bold, the rest quiet
colors = [RED if c == "mixed" else GREY
          for c in df["category"]]
ax.barh(df["category"], df["value"], color=colors)

# 2) DROP THE FRAME — only the bottom axis carries scale
for side in ["left", "right", "top"]:
    ax.spines[side].set_visible(False)
ax.tick_params(left=False)

# 3) MUTED GRID, X-AXIS ONLY
ax.grid(axis="x", alpha=0.3, linewidth=0.6)

# 4) LABEL THE BARS, DROP THE LEGEND
ax.bar_label(ax.containers[0],
             labels=[f"{v:.0%}" for v in df["value"]],
             padding=8, color=INK)

# 5) DESCRIPTIVE TITLE
fig.suptitle("Mixed training is gaining in popularity",
             fontsize=14, fontweight="bold", color=INK,
             x=0.04, ha="left")
```
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.6
import matplotlib.ticker as mtick
df = pd.DataFrame({
    "category": ["speed", "strength", "endurance", "mixed"],
    "value":    [0.10,    0.21,        0.27,        0.42],
})
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4.6))
colors = [RED if c == "mixed" else GREY for c in df["category"]]
ax.barh(df["category"], df["value"], color=colors)
for side in ["left", "right", "top"]:
    ax.spines[side].set_visible(False)
ax.tick_params(left=False)
ax.grid(axis="x", alpha=0.3, linewidth=0.6); ax.set_axisbelow(True)
ax.bar_label(ax.containers[0],
             labels=[f"{v:.0%}" for v in df["value"]],
             padding=8, fontsize=10, color=INK)
ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(mtick.PercentFormatter(1, decimals=0))
ax.set_xlim(0, 0.55)
fig.suptitle("Mixed training is gaining in popularity",
             fontsize=13, fontweight="bold", color=INK, x=0.04, ha="left", y=0.97)
fig.text(0.04, 0.90, "Share of athletes by primary training mode, 2024",
         fontsize=10, color=MUTED)
plt.tight_layout(rect=[0, 0, 1, 0.88])
plt.show()
```
:::
::::

::: {.takeaway}
[The bottom line]{.tl}
**Color carries the story.** Spend the loud colour on the row that matters and
let everything else fade into context — frames, ticks, and legends disappear.
:::

<small>Adapted from [*Make Your Charts Look Glorious*](https://medium.com/data-science/make-your-charts-look-glorious-9ce3fa310b70).</small>

## A Dumbbell for QC {.smaller}

[Make it publication-ready]{.eyebrow}

### The job: summarise sequencing QC to your boss

You sent 12 samples for sequencing. For each, you have the **raw mapping rate** and the **callable rate after QC**. The boss wants one chart: which samples held up, and which lost too much.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
Start with the data, one row per sample, sorted so the worst callable rate sits at the bottom.

```{.python code-line-numbers="1-4"}
qc = load_qc()                       # 12 samples
qc = qc.sort_values("callable")      # worst at the bottom
y  = range(len(qc))                  # one row each
qc.head()
```
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| class-output: df-preview
qc = load_qc().sort_values("callable").reset_index(drop=True)
y = range(len(qc))
print(qc[["sample", "raw", "callable", "loss"]].head())
```
:::
::::

<!-- slide 57 -->
## A Dumbbell for QC {.smaller}

[Make it publication-ready]{.eyebrow}

### Draw the bars: the gap is the story

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
One horizontal bar per sample, from callable to raw. The bar length *is* the QC loss, longer means more lost.

```{.python code-line-numbers="1|3-5"}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 5))

for i, r in qc.iterrows():            # one bar per row
    ax.plot([r.callable, r.raw],      # x: callable -> raw
            [i, i], color=GREY, lw=2)
```
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 5), facecolor=CREAM); ax.set_facecolor(CREAM)
for i, r in qc.iterrows():
    ax.plot([r.callable, r.raw], [i, i], color=GREY, lw=2, zorder=1)
ax.set_yticks(list(y)); ax.set_yticklabels(qc["sample"])
ax.set_xlim(60, 100)
ax.spines[["top", "right", "left"]].set_visible(False); ax.tick_params(left=False)
plt.show()
```
:::
::::

<!-- slide 58 -->
## A Dumbbell for QC {.smaller}

[Make it publication-ready]{.eyebrow}

### Add the dumbbell ends: raw and callable

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
Two dots per row: where the sample started (raw) and where it landed after QC (callable).

```{.python code-line-numbers="6-7"}
for i, r in qc.iterrows():
    ax.plot([r.callable, r.raw],
            [i, i], color=GREY, lw=2)

ax.scatter(qc.raw, y, color=GREY)        # raw mapping
ax.scatter(qc.callable, y, color=GREEN)  # callable after QC
```
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 5), facecolor=CREAM); ax.set_facecolor(CREAM)
for i, r in qc.iterrows():
    ax.plot([r.callable, r.raw], [i, i], color=GREY, lw=2, zorder=1)
ax.scatter(qc.raw, list(y), color=GREY, s=55, zorder=2)
ax.scatter(qc.callable, list(y), color=GREEN, s=55, zorder=3)
ax.set_yticks(list(y)); ax.set_yticklabels(qc["sample"])
ax.set_xlim(60, 100)
ax.spines[["top", "right", "left"]].set_visible(False); ax.tick_params(left=False)
```

## A Dumbbell for QC {.smaller}

[Make it publication-ready]{.eyebrow}

### The message: one bold colour flags the problem

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
A sample that loses more than 15 points is a concern. Colour those bars and dots **red**, everything else stays quiet. The eye goes straight to S01 and S12.

```{.python code-line-numbers="1|3-4|6-7"}
qc["flag"] = qc.loss > 15            # the rule

bar = [RED if f else GREY for f in qc.flag]
dot = [RED if f else GREEN for f in qc.flag]

ax.set_title("Two samples lose too much to QC",
             fontweight="bold", loc="left")
```
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5
import matplotlib.ticker as mtick
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 5), facecolor=CREAM); ax.set_facecolor(CREAM)
qc["flag"] = qc.loss > 15
for i, r in qc.iterrows():
    ax.plot([r.callable, r.raw], [i, i],
            color=RED if r.flag else GREY, lw=2, zorder=1)
ax.scatter(qc.raw, list(y), color=GREY, s=55, zorder=2, label="raw mapping")
ax.scatter(qc.callable, list(y),
           color=[RED if f else GREEN for f in qc.flag], s=55, zorder=3,
           label="callable after QC")
ax.set_yticks(list(y)); ax.set_yticklabels(qc["sample"])
ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(mtick.PercentFormatter(100, decimals=0))
ax.set_xlim(60, 100); ax.set_xlabel("genome callable")
ax.set_title("Two samples lose too much to QC", fontweight="bold", color=INK, loc="left")
ax.grid(axis="x", color=LINE, alpha=0.5, lw=0.6); ax.set_axisbelow(True)
ax.spines[["top", "right", "left"]].set_visible(False); ax.tick_params(left=False)
plt.show()
```
:::
::::

::: {.takeaway}
[The bottom line]{.tl}
A dumbbell turns "before vs after" into one readable picture. Sort by the value that matters, and let **one bold colour** carry the verdict.
:::

## General-Purpose Libraries {.smaller}

[The Python viz stack]{.eyebrow}

### Matplotlib · Seaborn · Plotly

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5

import matplotlib.patches as mpatches

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(10, 5))

# ── matplotlib ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
np.random.seed(42)
x = np.linspace(0, 4 * np.pi, 200)
axes[0].plot(x, np.sin(x), color=BRAND, linewidth=2.5, label='sin(x)')
axes[0].plot(x, np.cos(x), color=ACCENT_PURP, linewidth=2.5, label='cos(x)')
axes[0].fill_between(x, np.sin(x), alpha=0.15, color=BRAND)
axes[0].set_title('Matplotlib\n(low-level control)', fontsize=11)
axes[0].legend(fontsize=9)

# ── seaborn ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
df  = pd.DataFrame({'x': rng.normal(0, 1, 300), 'y': rng.normal(0, 1, 300),
                    'group': rng.choice(['A','B','C'], 300)})
for g, color in zip(['A','B','C'], [BRAND, ACCENT_YLW, ACCENT_PURP]):
    sub = df[df['group'] == g]
    axes[1].scatter(sub['x'], sub['y'], color=color, s=25, alpha=0.6, label=g)
axes[1].set_title('Seaborn\n(statistical plots)', fontsize=11)
axes[1].legend(fontsize=9)

# ── plotly badge (static preview) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
categories = ['Control', 'Treatment A', 'Treatment B', 'Treatment C']
values     = [45, 78, 62, 91]
bars = axes[2].barh(categories, values,
                    color=[GRAY_DARK, BRAND, BRAND_LIGHT, ACCENT_YLW])
axes[2].set_xlim(0, 110)
for bar, val in zip(bars, values):
    axes[2].text(val + 2, bar.get_y() + bar.get_height()/2,
                 f'{val}', va='center', fontsize=9)
axes[2].set_title('Plotly\n(interactive plots)', fontsize=11)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.footer style="font-size: 0.55em; color: #808080; white-space: nowrap;"}
All three libraries are installed with: `pip install matplotlib seaborn plotly`
:::

## Setting Up Your Environment {.smaller .scrollable}

[The Python viz stack]{.eyebrow}

### One command installs everything

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="52%"}
```bash
# 1. Clone the course repo
git clone <course-repo-url> dataviz-genomicsdata
cd dataviz-genomicsdata

# 2. Fresh conda env (recommended)
conda create -n genomeviz python=3.11 -y
conda activate genomeviz

# 3. Install the course package — this pulls
#    EVERY dependency declared in
#    genomics_course/pyproject.toml
pip install -e genomics_course/

# 4. Build the teaching datasets once
#    (writes parquets under
#     genomics_course/data/files/)
python -m genomics_course.data._build
```
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
::: fragment
```python
# Verify the install
from genomics_course.theme import *
from genomics_course.data import (
    load_deseq2, load_admixture,
    load_microbiome, load_expression,
    load_pseudotime, load_wine,
)

print(load_deseq2().shape)      # (15000, 5)
print(load_microbiome().shape)  # (96, 4)
print(load_expression().shape)  # (40, 24)
print(load_pseudotime().shape)  # (2000, 3)
```
:::

::: fragment
::: {.takeaway}
A single `pip install -e genomics_course/`
brings in matplotlib, seaborn, plotly, scipy,
scikit-learn, scanpy, umap-learn,
PyComplexHeatmap, pyCirclize, toytree,
pywaffle, gget, biopython, adjustText,
networkx, ternary-diagram, squarify,
pypalettes — **no per-package pip install.**
:::
:::
:::

## Where to Run the Code {.smaller .scrollable}

[The Python viz stack · pick your platform]{.eyebrow}

### Three ways to use the course package

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="33%"}
**Google Colab** — cloud, zero local setup

```python
# Run inside a Colab cell
!git clone <course-repo-url>
%cd dataviz-genomicsdata
!pip install -e genomics_course/
!python -m genomics_course.data._build
```

Open a fresh notebook at
`colab.research.google.com`,
paste the cell above, run once.
Re-run on every new Colab session
(VMs are ephemeral).
:::

::: {.column width="33%"}
**JupyterLab** — local notebook

```bash
# In a terminal, once
conda create -n genomeviz \
  python=3.11 -y
conda activate genomeviz
pip install -e genomics_course/
pip install jupyterlab
python -m genomics_course.data._build

# Launch
jupyter lab
```

In JupyterLab, **Kernel →
Change Kernel → genomeviz**
so notebooks see the install.
:::

::: {.column width="33%"}
**VS Code** — IDE + notebooks

```bash
# In a terminal, once
conda create -n genomeviz \
  python=3.11 -y
conda activate genomeviz
pip install -e genomics_course/
python -m genomics_course.data._build

# Open the repo
code .
```

In VS Code: **⇧⌘P → Python:
Select Interpreter → genomeviz**.
For `.ipynb` files, also pick
`genomeviz` from the kernel
selector at the top right.
:::
::::::

The install is **the same** everywhere — only the launcher differs.
Colab clones in-notebook; Jupyter/VS Code assume a local clone.
